item.title: Police fire tear gas, arrest dozens as France sees more protests
item.description:
French police have arrested dozens and fired tear gas at some protestors Saturday as authorities stepped up security in major cities, aiming to prevent a repeat of last week's rioting. The nationwide demonstrations are focused on the high cost of living, and a massive turnout is expected again after more than half a million took to the streets last week.
France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 135 people have been arrested and a variety of weapons have been seized. The items confiscated include metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said. Nuñez added that, so far, "there has been no major incident" in the country.
Nuñez previously said as many as 70,000 officers will be deployed nationwide, along with helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.
Demonstrations had been banned in the southeast city of Lyon, but about 150 protesters near the city's center briefly tried to block a road. Police fired tear gas to disperse the group. A 21-year-old student, who spoke to the Agence France-Presse on the condition of anonymity, described authorities as "really mobile."
"They come and disperse marches before they even form," the student said. A police helicopter was seen flying over the city, and security forces, armored vehicles and riot police vans were patrolling.

item.title: Deadly shooting in Paris suburb investigated as terrorism, officials say
item.description:
A gunman shooting from his car killed one person and injured at least 5 others, including a 12-year-old girl, in the Paris suburb of Trappes on Friday, in what authorities described as a racially motivated act of terrorism.
President Emmanuel Macron called it "a racist terror attack" and said the suspect's statements suggested it was premeditated.
"These people were targeted because of their skin color or perceived religion, and for no other reason," Macron said following a meeting with officials and residents. "There is no place for this in France."
Prosecutors said they were investigating whether the acts targeted the "real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion" of the victims. They said they have opened an investigation for "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise."
The alleged shooter was "firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath" as he drove through Trappes and neighboring La Verriere, Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh told broadcaster BFMTV.
"This is probably one of the first attempted mass killings motivated by Islamophobia and racism," Rabeh told reporters, the Associated Press reported. "This was a terrorist attack with racist, likely Islamophobic, overtones."
Police officers at the scene of a shooting rampage that killed at least 1 in Trappes, a suburb of Paris, France, on Oct, 23, 2026.
Dimitar DILKOFF /AFP via Getty Images
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the suspect fired "what appears to have been a military-grade weapon, or at least an automatic weapon." Rabeh called it a "miracle" that there were not more casualties. Nuñez said the gunman "clearly" committed "a terrorist crime" that may have been racially motivated.

item.title: Iran says U.S. military not allowed in Gulf "under any circumstance"
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: Iran warned on Saturday that U.S. ships would never be allowed in the Persian Gulf "under any circumstances," as tensions between Tehran and Washington continue mounting. Both sides have signalled a possible return to strikes, with the U.S. ambassador to Turkey warning Iran could be struck as soon as this weekend.Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz has told the Financial Times the war with Iran could last another year, but Waltz said he hopes the Iranians "come to the table" before that.
New Updates

Yemen's Houthis claim attack on Aden naval base, military camp
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis claimed an attack Saturday on a naval base and a military camp in Aden, the interim seat of the internationally recognized government, after blasts were heard there.
"Our armed forces targeted Saudi enemy concentrations at the so-called Al-Nasr camp and the naval base in Aden," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said, adding the sites were overseen by Saudi forces.
The Houthis fighting the Saudi-backed government have targeted the southern city several times in recent weeks, including the presidential palace.
The Houthis said they attacked a Saudi position in Aden on Wednesday, with smoke seen rising near the city's airport.

item.title: 1 arrested after fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest mountain retreat
item.description:
A suspect has been arrested in Germany following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as Eagle's Nest, German police said.
Authorities were alerted to a fire at the Nazi leader's mountain residence on the peak of Obersalzberg at approximately 9:15 p.m. local time on Friday, Upper Bavaria South police said in a statement.
The building, also known as Kehlsteinhaus, was "completely engulfed in flames" when firefighters arrived, police said, but no one was found inside and no injuries were reported.
Fire trucks had some difficulty accessing the site "due to the local conditions," authorities added.
Still from a webcam of the Kehlsteinhaus early on Oct. 24, 2026, after a large fire broke out in the southern German state of Bavaria.
Berchtesgaden /AFP via Getty Images
"Shortly after the fire broke out, a suspect came into the focus of investigators," the statement said, adding that the cause of the fire is now under criminal investigation and one person was taken into custody.
The 33-year-old suspect, a German citizen who has ties to the Berchtesgaden area but doesn't currently live there, prosecutors said, has been questioned, The Associated Press reported. They said he showed signs of mental illness and he was being sent to a psychiatric facility, but they also would look into the possibility of a political motive in view of the building's history.
There were no current indications that anyone else was involved, police said.
At an elevation of 6,017 feet, Hitler's Eagle's Nest was completed in 1938 and occasionally used by the Nazi leader as a temporary seat of government. The site was spared from Allied bombing during World War II, largely preserving its original state.

item.title: Ukraine says Starlink speed restored after long disruption
item.description:
Ukraine's military has regained full use of Starlink satellite links for its drones and other fast-moving equipment, the defense minister said Saturday, ending speed restrictions that Ukrainian officials said had disrupted front-line operations for more than a week.
The Defense Ministry's monitoring systems in Ukraine reported stable connections on objects traveling faster than 250 mph, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told reporters.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that checks were conducted and it was determined Starlink and Starshield were running at the correct speed.
"Now the speed is what we need," Zelenskyy said. "The restoration began last night, and in the morning there were already speeds sufficient to use this connection. This is very important."
"This is significant for our front-line logistics, for protecting Ukraine from reactive 'Shaheds,'" he continued, referring to the Iranian-made drones regularly launched by Russia.
The limitations placed on Starshield — SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service and the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication — last week alarmed the country's military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Oct. 22, 2026.
Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images
The restoration comes as U.S. envoys launched a new push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.

item.title: U.K. police confirm it received letter with claims against Meghan's father
item.description:
A letter making a "number of claims" against the father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was received by the Metropolitan Police in 2019, a Scotland Yard spokesperson confirmed to CBS News on Saturday.
Police said they passed the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess "for their awareness," however, the details of the allegations made in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.
On Friday, it was reported that Meghan's father, Thomas Markle, is under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials.
The British tabloid The Sun reported Thursday that Thomas Markle, who has been estranged from his daughter for years, had been reported to authorities in the Philippines by his son, Thomas Markle Jr., after the younger man allegedly discovered child abuse materials in storage boxes at his father's home in the Philippines.
Thomas Markle, Meghan's father, is seen in a still taken from a video as he gives an interview to ITV's "Good Morning Britain" program on June 18, 2018.
REUTERS
The Daily Mail reported Friday that Markle had denied the allegations against him.
Meghan, who recently moved back to Britain with her husband Prince Harry and their children, said in a statement sent to CBS News on Friday that she was "deeply distressed" by reports about her father. She said she had been aware of the allegations against him since 2018 and that the allegations were shared with U.K. authorities at the time.

item.title: Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns
item.description:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East, and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.
Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
Axios was first to report on the memo.
The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.

item.title: Melania Trump secures "temporary ceasefire" in Ukrainian city
item.description:
First lady Melania Trump's office on Friday said she — not President Trump or another top official — has secured a temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine for the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky for humanitarian reasons.
In an unusual announcement for a first lady's office, it said both nations agreed to temporarily halt all military action in the southern Ukrainian city "to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway." The localized ceasefire will begin Thursday, Oct. 29.
Russia and Ukraine have not commented on the first lady's announcement. But Ukrainian officials indicated that there has been a tentative agreement in the Russian-occupied territory in southern Ukraine.
The first lady's office says she worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire."
"The situation in Oleshky is dire," the first lady said in a statement. "Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water. The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible."
The first lady's office said she "initiated discussions with both nations and aligned the parties on the agreement's objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary."
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," the first lady said.
